To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) pollen, plant macro- and geochemical analyses provide detailed insights into early Holocene vegetation development in a sunken landscape of the Borkum-Riffgrund, southern part of the North Sea; (ii) pollen, plant and geochemical analyses indicate that the landscape of the Bormum Riffgrund was covered with Pinus–Carylus woodland, followed by the development of an Alnus–Salix carr; (iii) the landscape was flooded by the rising

a vibrocore from 33 m below present sea-level in the Borkumariffgrund, southernmost North Sea, provided a ~1,600-year record of early-Holocene vegetation history and landscape development in the southernmost North Sea.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the palaeoecology of a sunken landscape and the development of coastal mires.
the paludification and marine inundation of sunken landscapes, and with the application of new analytical methods to identify key horizons for the dating of such sequences.
the early Holocene history of a sunken landscape and its palaeoecology, as well as with the development of new dating methods and their applicability in palaeoenvironmental research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pollen, plant macro-fossils and geochemical methods provide complementary information and are therefore indispensable for the reconstruction of the environmental history of sun-ken landscapes.

the Borkum vibrocore provides a unique record of early Holucene vegetation and landscape development on sunken grounds of the southern North sea, and that the application of pollen, plant macro fossil and geochemical methods is a powerful tool to reconstruct the environmental history of sunke landscapes.
the early Holocene vegetation and mire history in this area of the southern North sea can be reconstructed with a high resolution of 10–20 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combined application of botanical, geochemical and sedimentological methods provides the most detailed insights into the early Holocene environmental history in a landscape which has sunk below sea-level.
the combined application of botanical methods and geochemistry provides the most comprehensive results for palaeoecological and palaeoenvironmental reconstructions.

the combined use of pollen, plant macro-fossil, XRF-Scans, XRF-Measurements, and geochemical analyses provides a detailed and reliable record of early Holucene environmental history of sunke landscapes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the early Holocene vegetation development of a sunken landscape can be reconstructed with pollen and plant macrofossils from a vibrocore.

the Borkum-Riffgrund sequence provides a valuable reference for the early Holocene environmental history in the southern North Sea and for understanding of the development and dynamics of sunken landscapes in general.
the Borkum-Riffgrund core provides a unique record of early Holocen vegetation and mire development, and of sea-level change, in a now submerged landscape.
